instances.title: Hybrid work-from-home policy experiment (Trip.com, Nature 2024)
instances.problem: Can we predict the impact of two work-from-home days?
instances.situation: In August 2021 Trip.com let half of 1,612 Airfare and IT employees in Shanghai work from home on Wednesdays and Fridays for six months; the other half stayed in the office. Who was offered was decided by birthday, so the two groups are directly comparable.
instances.data_used: The experiment's public replication deposit (Nature 2024): one row per employee with commute, family, tenure, role and manager status, plus the measured outcomes: who quit, the endline survey, performance grades and how often home days were taken.
instances.protocol_line: Simulation predictions use employee information from before the policy and assumptions from earlier research. Actual outcomes are used to check accuracy.
instances.intro: Simulates the 1,612 employees of Trip.com's 2021 hybrid-work experiment as digital twins over six months: half were offered Wednesdays and Fridays at home, half were not. Each twin decides weekly whether to work from home and whether to stay, from its own commute, family, preferences and team. The prediction is scored against the randomized experiment; the alternatives explore offering hybrid work to everyone and adding an AI assistant for customer replies and analysis.
instances.world: 1,612 employees in two divisions over six months (Aug 2021 to Jan 2022). Half were randomly offered two WFH days a week. Every real employee is simulated as a digital twin built from their own covariates; outcomes are attrition, satisfaction, performance and the manager contrast, scored at the population level against the randomized experiment.

instances.title: U.S. federal workforce separations after the 2025 changes (OPM data)
instances.problem: Can we predict how many employees each federal agency loses after a return-to-office order and a paid resignation offer?
instances.situation: On 20 January 2025 the President ordered federal agencies to end remote work, and on 28 January OPM offered nearly every federal employee a deferred resignation: stop working, stay paid until 30 September 2025, then leave. The offer closed on 12 February.
instances.data_used: OPM's Federal Workforce Data: every separation from federal service by month since 2005 (agency, age band, length of service, type of separation) and monthly snapshots of all 2.3 million employees, published through a public API.
instances.protocol_line: Each agency's employees are simulated from the December 2024 snapshot and separation rates before 2025, with assumptions from earlier research. Later separations are scored separately; source revisions prevent a claim of information available beforehand.
instances.intro: Simulates the 2.3 million civilian federal employees in OPM's data as cohort twins (one per agency, age band, length of service, appointment, schedule and supervisory status), each with its own pre-2025 separation rates by type. The return-to-office order raises voluntary leaving and the deferred resignation offer is taken up by the employees most likely to leave anyway, as a one-off early-retirement window does. Separations by agency and month from February to December 2025 are scored against what OPM recorded; the alternative asks what the return-to-office order would have done without the resignation offer.
instances.world: Federal civilian employees in OPM's data, as of December 2024, grouped into cohort twins by agency, age band, length of service, appointment, work schedule and supervisory status. Separations by type follow each twin's own pre-change rates; the 2025 return-to-office order and the deferred resignation offer enter on their announced dates. Outcomes are separations by agency and month, February to December 2025.

instances.title: AI adoption by sector (Census BTOS)
instances.company: U.S. employer businesses in the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey
instances.problem: Can we predict what share of businesses in each sector will be using AI three and six months from now?
instances.protocol_line: Every prediction is made from survey periods before its cutoff and scored on the periods three and six months after it; the design was frozen on the first quarter of the cutoffs.
instances.situation: From September 2023 the Census Bureau asked businesses every two weeks whether they had used AI in producing goods or services in the last two weeks. Use rose in every sector, fastest in information, professional services and finance.
instances.data_used: The Business Trends and Outlook Survey's biweekly estimates of the share of businesses that used AI, by two-digit NAICS sector, from September 2023 until the question's wording changed in November 2025 (public domain, U.S. Census Bureau).
instances.intro: Rebuilds U.S. businesses as populations of firms, one population per sector. Each period a firm that does not use AI may start, and a firm that uses it may stop, with hazards that follow a diffusion curve: firms imitate adopters in their own sector and in the whole economy, and growth can slow as fewer non-users remain. From each cutoff the simulation carries every sector forward and is scored against the share of firms that actually reported AI use three and six months later. The alternative asks how much faster manufacturing and retail would adopt if an adoption programme doubled their firms' hazard of starting.
instances.world: Fifteen sectors, each a population of 1,000 simulated firms that use AI or not; the national share of firms using AI is the economy-wide signal that firms in every sector imitate.

instances.title: A knowledge business after ChatGPT (Stack Overflow)
instances.company: Stack Overflow, the question-and-answer site for programmers
instances.problem: Can we predict how many questions developers will ask on Stack Overflow in the next three to six months, as AI assistants take over?
instances.protocol_line: Every prediction is made from weeks before its cutoff and scored on the 26 weeks after it; the design was frozen on the first quarter of the cutoffs.
instances.situation: OpenAI released ChatGPT on 30 November 2022. Within a year developers were asking AI assistants the questions they used to post on Stack Overflow, and weekly new questions fell by more than half.
instances.data_used: Weekly counts of new Stack Overflow questions from March 2021 to October 2026, from the public Stack Exchange API (content CC BY-SA; counts exclude deleted questions).
instances.intro: Rebuilds Stack Overflow's question flow as a population of would-be askers. Each week every asker who still posts questions may switch to an AI assistant, and some switch back, with hazards that follow a diffusion curve calibrated on the weeks before the cutoff; the questions that reach the site are the pre-ChatGPT trend and seasonality times the askers who have not switched. Predictions are scored against the questions actually posted in the 13 and 26 weeks after each cutoff, and from the launch week itself. The alternative asks how many questions the site would have kept if the switch to AI assistants had gone half as fast.
instances.world: Stack Overflow's would-be askers as one population of 1,000 simulated developers who post their questions on the site or ask an AI assistant instead; the question volume without AI comes from the trend and seasonality before the launch.
